doc.title: Ramsey Lewis — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Ray Charles and the gospel influence
summary: Lewis says Ray Charles' turn to gospel touched him, though he met him only once.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: I was referencing pretty much the gospel influence that was coming. We look at Ray Charles. Already by 1956, Hallelujah, I love her so. Just that one pronoun changed it
from being a gospel tune to being an r-and-b tune. So there seemed to have been, if not a zeitgeist, at least an influx of the gospel church influence into the music, and Jimmy Smith.

Ray Charles was an influence. I think the reason he was an influence is because early Ray Charles, he was doing Charles Brown. He was doing Nat Cole. Right? But then he found this thing. He took gospel music as a source, and he did it so well. You’re right. Those songs, Drown in My Own Tears and The Nighttime is the Right Time and – the list goes on and on. I bought all of his records, because I think he touched me in that place where, when I was playing in our church and the people would testify, or they would sing, and I was so young. He touched something there. In fact, I recorded a song called Salute to Ray Charles, a long time ago.
Did you get to know him?
I think I met Ray Charles once, but no, I did not get to know him.
